BIG CARNIVAL AT EASTON
Easton, Md., August 5. — A big carnival was held at the Fair Grounds last Thursday. A baseball game between the Oxford team and the Easton Speed Skids proved a big attraction. The Easton Lyric Concert Band furnished music for the occasion.

Rev. J. W Butler filled the pulpit at Asbury M. E. Church Sunday morning.

Mrs. Lizzie Bailey and neice, Miss Della Cooper, spent Saturday and Sunday at Longwoods.

The Colored Laboring Men's Association held a business meeting last Thursday.

Mrs. Kate Johnson, of St Michaels, spent Sunday with her mother, Mrs Hennie Camper.

Irene Hawkins, a maid employed in the Savoy Hotel, Nashville, Tenn., was brutally assaulted and then murdered on Sunday of last week. E. J. Seymour, white, who says he is a traveling salesman, is charged with the crime. The seventeenth annual session of the Alabama State Federation of Colored Women's Clubs, was held

in Selma, recently. Reports showed that the Federation handled nearly $5,000 during the past year.

Three colored persons were on the ill-fated Eastland, when she turned over at her wharf in Chicago last Saturday morning. They were: Miss Eva Braxton, Paul Martin and William Robinson. All escaped unhurt, although Miss Braxton is at present ill at her home as a result of the shock.

The National Association of Photographers held its annual meeting in Indianpolis, Ind., last week. T. C. Patton, a local photographer, was the only colored representative.

irene-hawkins-nashville-1915-07-25.A5:
Criminals Confined to No Particular Race.
Nashville, Tenn., Aug. 10.—Charged with brutally assaulting and then murdering Irene Hawkins, a colored girl employed as a chamber maid in the Savoy hotel, Seventh avenue, N. E. J. Seymour, purporting to be a traveling man from Chicago, Ill., stopping at that hostelry, is being held by Murder Officers Jay Newsum and George Carter in bonds of $2,500.

Sunday afternoon, July 25, the girl was seen in the room occupied by Seymour, where she was performing her duties as chamber maid. Twenty minutes later the girl's body was discovered, bruised and mangled, in the alleyway directly underneath the window of the room occupied by Seymour. Patrolman Carney found Seymour at the station, just about to board a train for Chicago, and put him under arrest.

The coroner started an investigation on Monday and on Tuesday his jury returned a verdict charging Seymour with violating the girl and then murdering her. Ada Stokes, another maid at the hotel, testified that Seymour, a few days earlier, had attempted to keep her in the room with him, but that she refused, and that she barely escaped from the room before he could succeed in locking the door on her. After that she took pains to see that the man was absent from the room before she entered it. The evidence showed that Seymour had evidently beaten and assaulted the girl before throwing her from the window.

JEWS SPILL GORE
IN WILD RIOT
When an unknown Negro slashed the strings of a woman's handbag as she alighted from a Fourteenth car at Hastings and Division-sts., early Sunday evening, he started a race riot that threatened to assume serious proportions before the police checked it.

The Negro's act was witnessed by several Jewish lads in the neighborhood, who shouted an alarm. The Negro dropped the handbag and vaulted through an open window of a passing car. A companion escaped down a side street.

In half a minute a crowd had formed. Someone pulled the trolley off and brought the car to a stop. The other passengers left hurriedly, leaving the Negro is undisputed possession. He stood defying the mob with a large knife, which he brandished threateningly.

Sam Smith, of No. 229 Adelaide-st., was braver than the rest. He volunteered to bring forth the Negro, single-handed. He came back alone, with a knife wound in his back and bloodstains all over his Sunday shirt.

The Negro stood on the rear platform, keeping the angry crowd at bay till Charles Hamilton, Negro, of No. 189 Division-st., came to his assistance with a revolver.

"You better back up till I get this man out of here," cried Hamilton.

At the same instant a crowd of 25 Negroes pounced on the Jews from the rear. The latter fled down Hastings-st., with the Negroes, armed with knives, revolvers and bricks, in aggressive pursuit.

Max Reisman, No. 227 Montcalm-st. east, was stabbed about the face and scalp and went to St. Mary's. Benjamin Jeffrey, of No. 372 Monroe-ave., was shot through the foot by an unknown person.

Detective William Rick traced Hamilton and the robber to the former's rooming house on Division-st. Hamilton pressed a revolver to the detective's stomach and threatened to shoot but Rick wrested it from him. During the scuffle the other man escaped. DETROIT, Aug. 2. — Above the usual din in Hastings street last night could be heard the roar of a race riot between 50 Jews and twice as many negroes.

When 15 detectives and patrolmen had quelled the disturbance, one man had been shot and two men and a woman had been stabbed. Five arrests were made.

Jewish boys saw a negro steal a woman's handbag. They gave the alarm and the negro boarded a street car.

All the passengers but the thief fled. He pulled a long knife and held the fort. One of a crowd of Hebrew besiegers went in to get him, but he brought away severe slashes instead.

Then negro re-enforcements arrived. Half the new force charged the Jews from the front and the others in the rear. In a few moments the entire Jewish contingent was racing down the street with the superior force of blacks pursuing.

Policemen finally broke up the battle.

100 NEGROES ROUT 60 JEWS.
Black Steals Purse in Ghetto District at Detroit.
Detroit, Mich., Aug. 2—High above the usual din in Hastings street could be heard the roar of a race riot between 50 Jews and twice as many negroes. When 15 detectives and patrolmen had quelled the disturbance, one man had been shot and two men and a woman had been stabbed. Five arrests were made. Several small boys, sons of Jewish merchants, saw two negroes steal a woman's handbag and gave an alarm. The negroes fled, pursued by a crowd. One negro boarded a passing street car. The trolley was pulled off and the car surrounded.

GIRL ACCUSES NEGRO
Annabel Denny Tells Story Of Fighting Assailant
Fighting Assailant

Easton, Md., Aug. 28—Robert Smith, a young negro, is in jail here on the charge of having assaulted Annabel Denny, 15-year-old daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Elbert L. Denny, at her home near Royal Oak last Tuesday night, and the feeling against against the accused here in the county is so strong that State's Attorney Charles J. Battler is trying to arrange for a speedy trial in order to prevent lynching.

The story of the assault did not get out until yesterday because Mr. Denny, though informed by daug-hter when he returned home, kept the matter quiet. He was greatly enraged and would have shot the negro had the latter been caught. Mrs. Denny came to Easton Thursday night and preferred the charge. Yesterday morning Sheriff Sewell and Deputy Sheriff Stevens went to Smith's house and found him in bed. robert-smith-easton-1915-08.A6:
WILL GIVE COURT CHANCE
TO PASS ON ASSAULT CASE
EASTON, Md., Aug. 30. — Since the people in and around Royal Oak, where Annabel Denny, the 13-year-old daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Elbert Denny, upon whom a criminal assault was committed at her home a few days ago by Robert Smith, colored, had definite assurance from State's Attorney Charles J. Butler that Judge Hopper, of this judicial circuit, would convene the grand jury for Talbot county on Wednesday or Thursday for the purpose of hearing the evidence in the case, all incipient talk of lynching was stopped. The neighbors of the Denny family have become more reconciled to the situation and everything is quiet in the locality. For a time, though, fear of a lynching kept the county authorities on the alert.

Sheriff Sewell is keeping a diligent watch on his prisoner to see that he does not escape and to see that no crowds loiter around the jail.

robert-smith-easton-1915-08.A9:
JURY INDICTS MEN
FOR VICIOUS ASSAULTS
EASTON, Md., Sept. 3.—The Talbot county grand jury has indicted James R. Smith, colored, for criminally assaulting Anna L. Denny, 13 years old, of Royal Oak, on August 22, and Aaron Johnson also colored, for criminally assaulting Mrs. Lulu Wiley, of St. Michaels, on August 2. Mrs. Willey is feeble-minded, which makes the crime even more serious. The penalty for conviction in both cases is death.

Court adjourned after receiving the indictments without fixing a date for trials. It will be fixed by Associate Judge Adkins, and will probably be about September 15.

It is the first time in the history of the county that a grand jury has been recalled to consider criminal matters after having been discharged. Judge Constable and Associate Judge Hopper presided today. The attendance was very large, but there was no evidence of disorder.
robert-smith-easton-1915-08.A11:
OUTRAGEOUS CRIME
A case similar to that for which "Wish" Sheppard was executed at Denton, has occurred in Talbot county. Annabel Denny, a fifteen-year-old daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Elbert L. Denny, near Royal Oak, Talbot county, Md., has accused Robert Smith, colored who is about seventeen years old, of criminal assault, and he is now under arrest in the county jail at Easton.

State's Attorney Charles J. Butler, said, that he anticipated nothing like mob violence, as the people of Talbot county are disposed to allow the law to take its course. Nevertheless, it is his purpose to bring the perpetrator to a speedy trial.

There is a doubt in Mr. Butler's mind from the evidence he has, whether the assault was entirely complete, though it appears the perpetrator's offense is sufficiently serious to put him in danger of the gallows. The Dennys are prominent people in Talbot county.

The girl's father was away at the time of the assault, but when he returned home would have shot the negro if he could have caught him,

Her father, for good reasons, kept the affair a secret, but her mother came to Eaaton Thursday night and laid charges against the negro, and early Friday morning Sheriff Sewell and Deputy Sheriff Stevens went to his home, found him in bed, put him under arrest, and brought him to Easton and put him in jail.

He was given a hearing before Police Justice Tharp. The feeling against him was so strong that State Attorney Butler went to Centreville to get Judge Hopper to call the Talbot county grand jury together at once and give the culprit a speedy trial.

Judge Hopper, of Centreville, ordered the grand jury for Talbot county to be convened in special session Thursday to hear the evidence against the negro.

The jury will also investigate the case of Aaron Joseph, a negro, who is charged with assault on Mrs. Lulu Willey, wife of Charles Willey, a farmer near St. Michaels. All is quiet in the localities where the crimes were committed, and there is no likelihood of trouble, since both accused men are to be speedily tried.
robert-smith-easton-1915-08.A12:
TO BE TRIED IN CECIL.
Assault Case Removed From Talbot County.
The Circuit Court for Talbot County met in special session at Easton on Friday with Chief Judge Constable and Associate Judges Adkins and Hopper on the bench, for the purpose of trying the cases of Robert J. Smith, colored, charged with criminal assault upon AnnaBell Denny, the 13-year-old daughter of Elbert L. Denny, of Royal Oak, on August 22, and Aaron Johnson, also colored, charged with a criminal assault upon Mrs. Lulu Willey, wife of Charles Willey, a farmer, living near St. Michaels, at her home August 2.

The case of Smith was taken up first. Smith's counsel, George H. Pendleton, colored, of Baltimore, filed an affidavit made by Smith before a notary public setting forth that he did not belive he could get a fair and impartial trial in Talbot county and moved to have the case removed to another county. The court agreed to send the case to the Circuit Court for Cecil County, and set Friday, September 24, as the day for trial.
In the case of Johnson, State's Attorney Butler, who brought the charge against him under the common law, moved that the indictment be quashed and that the prisoner be held in custody, as he had decided to try him under the statue law of Maryland. This case will not come up until court convenes again on the third Monday in November.
robert-smith-easton-1915-08.A14:
HIS YOUTH MAY SAVE
HIM FROM GALLOWS
ELKTON, Md., Sept. 25.—The case of James Robert Smith, colored, indicted by the Talbot county grand jury on the charge of criminal assault on Anna Lee Denny, a 13-year-old white girl, near Easton, and removed to Cecil county for trial, was concluded yesterday, but the court before whom the case was tried reserved its verdict until Monday afternoon.

In the meantime the testimony of the victim will be gone over carefully by the judges. The prisoner will be 17 years old next month, and he had been employed in the Denny family since he was a small child. Smith was brought to Elkton by Deputy Sheriff Stephenson of Easton, in an automobile yesterday. State's Attorney Butler of Easton, was assisted in the prosecution by State's Attorney Henry L. Constable of Elkton. On account of the youth of the prisoner, it is not thought the death penalty will be imposed should the court find him guilty.

will-leach-dade-city-1915-08-05.A15:
NINE MEN ARE MOBBED IN SOUTH IN ONE DAY IN SOUTH IN ONE DAY
MEMPHIS, Tenn., Aug. 7.—Within the last 24 hours nine negroes were hanged, seven legally and two lynched in southern states, and today a lynching party is pursuing a 10th negro near Liberty, Mo.

There were four legal hangings in Alabama. Robert Watkins and John Salter were executed for the murder of Mrs. Mary Lassiter at Evergreen. A militia guard prevented a mob from burning the negroes. The other two executions in Alabama were for the murder of white men.

At Fresno, Miss., Peter Bolen and Jim Seales, who killed another negro, were executed while 5,000 persons sang "There is a Land of Pure Delight."

Bunyan Walters was executed at Fayetteville, Miss.

A dispatch from Shawnee, Okla., relating the story of the lynching of Ed Berry, stated that the affair was "one of the most orderly lynchings in the history of the state." Berry was hanged from a railroad bridge and his body was riddled with bullets, after which the mob dispersed "in a quiet and orderly manner."

In Trilby, Fla., a crowd of citizens lynched Will Leach, accused of attacking a 13-year-old girl.

Early today a report from Liberty, Mo., stated that a lynching was almost certain if a mob caught a negro laborer who attacked a farmer's wife near there.
will-leach-dade-city-1915-08-05.A16:
Women See Executions and Crowd Sings Hymn-One Slayer Pursued.
MEMPHIS, Aug. 7.—Nine negroes were hanged, seven legally and two lynched, yesterday, in the southern states, while a tenth is being chased near Liberty, Mo., by a lynching party.

Alabama led the list with four legal hangings. The governor refused reprieves in each case. At Evergreen, Robert Watkins and John Salter were hanged while a squad of militiamen stood guard to prevent disorder, threatened by citizens who wanted the blacks burned for the murder and assault of Mrs. Mary Lassiter at Cullman.

George James was hanged for the murder of George Clayburn, who was shot through an open window while he was reading a Bible. Millard Carpenter was hanged at Birmingham for the murder two years ago of John T. Camp, a white man.

WOMEN ATTEND HANGING.

Mississippi hanged three negroes, but with two of them, Peter Bolen and Jim Seales, convicted of murdering another negro, an unusual spectacle was made. The hanging was at Fresco, the gallows being erected between two beautiful hills in a natural amphitheater.

Many women were in the crowd of 5,000 people and excursions were run from nearby towns. Just as the traps were sprung simultaneously the crowd burst forth into the hymn, "There Is a Land of Pure Delight," at the request of the negroes just before death.

Bunyan Walters was hanged at Fayetteville, Miss., for the murder of Tom Neals.

AN "ORDERLY MOB."

Dispatches from Shawnee, Okla., tell of a "quiet, orderly crowd armed to the teeth," which hanged Ed Berry to a Santa Fe railroad bridge, riddled his body with bullets and dispersed in as orderly a fashion as it had formed.

In the early morning hours at Trilby, Fla., a crowd, hypnotized with fury, lynched Will Leach, accused of attacking a 13-year-old girl.

At last reports a mob of 500 men were closing in on a negro near Liberty, Mo., who attacked a farmer's wife. Lynching is almost certain, it is said.
will-leach-dade-city-1915-08-05.A17:
LAW AND LYNCHERS TAKE NINE LIVES
Seven Negroes Legally Hanged and Two Killed by Mobs in South.
[By Telegraph to The Tribune.]
Tenn Aug. 6—Seven

Memphis, Tenn., Aug. 6.—Seven negroes were legally hanged and two were lynched in the South to-day. A mob from Liberty, Mo., is closing in tonight on a tenth man, who probably will be caught and killed before morning.

At Shawnee, Okla., Edward Berry, who confessed to assaults on twelve white women in the last three years, was taken at the pistol point from the hands of the Sheriff and his deputies by a masked mob of seventy men and hanged to a telegraph pole. Berry was being secretly brought into town to stand trial. In some way citizens heard of it and organized the quiet, determined mob that killed him. The negro was hanged near the Santa Fe Railway bridge, the scene of several of his crimes.

Frenzied over an assault on a thirteen-year-old girl, a big mob in Trilby, Fla., broke into the jail and dragged out and hanged Will Leach, suspected of the crime.

Four of the legal executions were in Alabama and two in Mississippi. At Evergreen, Ala., militia stood guard while Robert Watkins and John Salter were hanged for the murder of Mrs. Mary Lassiter. A crowd yelled and screamed to have the negroes burned.

In Starkville, Miss., two negro murderers were hanged. The authorities gave a barbecue for the crowd of spectators, at which lemonade and watermelon were served to about 5,000 farmers, while speeches were made by political candidates. Watermelon was served to the murderers just before they were led to the gallows.

Bloodhounds have been used to track down the negro who attacked Mrs. Henry Stafford near Liberty, Mo., yesterday. The man has been cornered in a patch of woodland, which has been surrounded. Several hundred men are after the criminal, and it is believed that he will be immediately lynched if caught.
